summary:
**AFTER THE SIGNAL** is a scientifically accurate digital space museum designed for children aged 6–14. We developed an Android application that brings the stories of human-made objects left on the Moon and Mars together in one accessible and interactive platform.

The application addresses the challenge of scattered, highly technical space information by transforming verified NASA data into age-appropriate documentary-style stories, interactive maps, and educational quizzes. Through a 2D solar system interface, children can explore six historical space objects, discover their scientific contributions, and understand what remains of these missions today. The content is available in Turkish and English, supports three age groups, and works offline, making space education more accessible.

This project is important because space exploration should be more than a collection of scientific achievements; it should also be a source of inspiration for future generations. By combining scientific accuracy, accessibility, and storytelling, AFTER THE SIGNAL turns forgotten mission hardware into an engaging educational experience and helps children understand that even when missions end, their discoveries continue to matter.
details:
Project Functionality, Benefits, Innovation and Development

How does it work?

AFTER THE SIGNAL is an Android application that functions as an interactive digital space museum. Users first select their age group and preferred language, then explore a 2D solar system by selecting the Moon or Mars. They can access interactive maps, discover six historical space objects, read documentary-style stories, examine technical information, and answer age-appropriate educational questions. The application combines NASA's verified data, images, mission records, and published coordinates to provide an informative experience.

What are its benefits and intended impact?

The project makes complex space exploration information accessible and engaging for children aged 6–14. It encourages scientific curiosity, develops awareness of space exploration history, and helps children understand the lasting scientific contributions of completed missions. Its offline functionality, lightweight 2D design, bilingual content, and accessibility features allow more children to benefit from space education, regardless of their device or internet access.

Our intended impact is to transform forgotten space mission objects into educational resources and inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and explorers.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project uses Android application development, NASA's open Image and Video Library API, NSSDCA records, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) coordinates, NASA Science and JPL mission records, and automated content-validation tests. The application uses a lightweight 2D architecture, local content storage, and offline functionality. Specific programming languages, development frameworks, and hardware are not specified in the project documentation.

How is the project creative and innovative?

Its main innovation is presenting the history of abandoned and remaining space mission equipment as an interactive digital museum rather than a conventional collection of scientific articles. It combines documentary storytelling, planetary exploration, historical maps, educational quizzes, and a laser retroreflector demonstration. It also emphasizes scientific honesty by distinguishing verified facts from imaginative narration and clearly identifying approximate locations and uncertain mission statuses.

What factors did the team consider?

We considered scientific accuracy, age-appropriate communication, accessibility, affordability, device compatibility, offline availability, bilingual support, and data privacy. We deliberately avoided unnecessary 3D graphics, advertisements, registration requirements, and competitive scoring systems. Our priority was to create an inclusive, reliable, lightweight, and educational experience that encourages curiosity rather than competition.
